subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: First, you learn to follow an algorithm (do the steps one by one) and understand it (say what job it does). Second, you learn to edit and correct an algorithm when a step is wrong or out of order. Third, you learn that the best algorithms are efficient and concise — they do the job in the fewest steps — and you learn to make instructions shorter by combining steps that repeat. Fourth, they move onto the computer and learn to make a simple Scratch program more concise, and to reset a character back to where it started.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Follow and understand an algorithm, and say what job it does.
Edit and correct an algorithm that has a wrong step or steps in the wrong order.
Understand that an efficient algorithm is concise — it uses the fewest steps.
Make instructions shorter by combining repeated steps and removing steps that are not needed.
In Scratch, build a short program and make it more concise.
In Scratch, add blocks to reset a sprite's position and size so a program can be run again and again.

concepts.title: What is an algorithm? Following and understanding
concepts.explanation:
An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job, and the steps must be in the right order. If you follow the steps one by one, you can understand what job the algorithm does, and check that it works.

When we make anjero, we do not just throw everything together. We do the steps in order. First we mix the batter. Then we let it rest. Then we heat the pan. Then we pour and cook.
concepts.example: Those steps in the right order are called an algorithm. Start with something you know.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you do the steps in order without skipping or adding steps? Do not worry yet about fixing mistakes — that is the next session.

concepts.title: Editing and correcting algorithms
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes an algorithm does not work. A step might be wrong, or two steps might be in the wrong order. We call a mistake like this a bug. When we find the bug we edit the algorithm (change it) to correct it.

A computer follows your steps exactly. If one step is wrong, the computer still does it, and you get the wrong answer.
concepts.example: It is not the computer's fault — it is a bug in our steps. Our job is to be a detective, find the wrong step, and fix it.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you point to the exact step that is wrong and say what it should be? Does you follow the steps first to test the algorithm, rather than guessing? Praise careful checking, not speed.

concepts.title: Making it concise: combining repeated steps
concepts.explanation:
The best algorithms are efficient — they do the job in the fewest steps. A short algorithm is concise. One easy way to make an algorithm concise is to look for steps that repeat, and combine them into one step.

Do what I say: clap, clap, clap. That was three steps. Is there a shorter way to say it?
concepts.example: Clap 3 times. That is what concise means — we said the same thing in a shorter way.
concepts.checkYourself: When you combine, Can you keep the same result (the right number of each thing)? A common slip is to write “pick 2 dates” when there were three — watch the counting. Can you spot which steps repeat?

concepts.title: Concise programs in Scratch
concepts.explanation:
The same idea works on the computer. In Scratch we join coloured blocks to make a program. If the same block repeats, we can often combine them into one block. This makes the program more concise.

our instructions. where we join them up. where it happens. Add the Balloon1 sprite using the Add Sprite button, and pick a simple backdrop like Blue Sky. Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create on the projector.

concepts.title: Resetting objects in Scratch
concepts.explanation:
In many games, a character goes back to the start after each go. We call this a reset. In Scratch, a program does not reset by itself. If we make a sprite move up or grow bigger, and then run the program again, it carries on from where it stopped — it floats off the top or grows too big. To fix this, we add blocks that put the sprite back to its starting position and size.

Think of a board game. After each go, you put the counter back on Start so you can play again.
concepts.example: Our sprite needs the same thing, or the second go begins in the wrong place. The problem makes the fix make sense.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you include the minus signs? Can you point to which block resets the position (go to x: y:) and which resets the size (set size to)? Does you run the program more than once to test the reset?

debugging.symptom: The order does not matter as long as all the steps are there.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: All the steps are there, but the order is silly. Order is part of the algorithm. Point it out: put your shoes on, then your socks.

debugging.fix: You often think more blocks means more work done, so it must be better. Show that the short version does the very same job — shorter is smarter here.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

selfAssessment: I can follow and understand an algorithm, and say what job it does.
I can edit and correct an algorithm that has a wrong step or steps in the wrong order.
I can understand that an efficient algorithm is concise — it uses the fewest steps.
I can make instructions shorter by combining repeated steps and removing steps that are not needed.
I can in Scratch, build a short program and make it more concise.
I can in Scratch, add blocks to reset a sprite's position and size so a program can be run again and again.
